pages.text: Inside the courtyard of the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, eleven-year-old Kwaku opened his history notebook beside his sister Abena. Before them stood a life-sized statue and archival photographs of a dignified Ashanti woman. ‘Welcome,’ said museum historian Curator Agyeman. ‘Today we are investigating the true historical story of Nana Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu.’

pages.alt: At the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, Kwaku and Abena stand with Curator Agyeman before a museum display of Nana Yaa Asantewaa.

pages.text: ‘Before we begin,’ Curator Agyeman said, holding up an old photograph and a notebook, ‘how do historians know what happened over a hundred years ago? We compare written records, colonial telegrams, photographs, museum artefacts, and Asante oral traditions passed down by elders. Where sources agree, we have established historical facts; where no word-for-word transcript was written down at the moment, historians say so honestly.’

pages.alt: Curator Agyeman shows Kwaku and Abena archival photographs and historical documents inside a glass display case.

pages.text: Curator Agyeman guided them to a display about nineteenth-century Asante. ‘Nana Yaa Asantewaa was born in the eighteen-forties in Besease near Ejisu,’ he explained. ‘In the Asante matrilineal system, the Queen Mother, or Ohemmaa, holds deep constitutional responsibility: she nominates the ruler, advises the council on peace and justice, and guards the welfare of the community.’

pages.alt: A museum painting shows Nana Yaa Asantewaa seated in council at Ejisu advising elders and community members.

pages.text: ‘By the eighteen-nineties,’ Curator Agyeman continued, ‘the British Empire sought control over the gold-rich Asante kingdom. In eighteen ninety-six, British troops entered Kumasi and arrested the Asantehene, Nana Prempeh the First, along with his mother Nana Yaa Akyaa and several chiefs, including Yaa Asantewaa’s own grandson, exiling them far away, first to Sierra Leone and later to the Seychelles islands in the Indian Ocean.’

In eighteen ninety-six, British troops entered Kumasi and arrested the Asantehene, Nana Prempeh the First, along with his mother Nana Yaa Akyaa and several chiefs, including Yaa Asantewaa’s own grandson, exiling them far away, first to Sierra Leone and later to the Seychelles islands in the Indian Ocean.’
pages.alt: A historical map display traces the long sea route from the Gold Coast to Sierra Leone and the Seychelles islands.

pages.text: Kwaku looked at a carved golden emblem in the gallery. ‘Even after exiling the King, what were the British still searching for?’ he asked. ‘The Golden Stool, Sika Dwa Kofi,’ said Curator Agyeman. ‘Since the time of Osei Tutu the First and Okomfo Anokye, the Golden Stool has been sacred to the Asante nation. It is never sat upon by anyone, not even the King. It represents the soul, unity and living spirit of the entire people.’

It is never sat upon by anyone, not even the King.
It represents the soul, unity and living spirit of the entire people.’
pages.alt: A museum exhibit illustrates the sacred Golden Stool resting on its own special throne cushion flanked by royal attendants.

pages.text: ‘On the twenty-eighth of March, nineteen hundred,’ said Curator Agyeman, ‘the British Governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, called a meeting of Asante leaders at the fort in Kumasi. In a speech recorded in British colonial dispatches, Hodgson declared that Nana Prempeh would not return and demanded that the Asante hand over the Golden Stool so that he, the Governor, could sit upon it!’
sentences: ‘On the twenty-eighth of March, nineteen hundred,’ said Curator Agyeman, ‘the British Governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, called a meeting of Asante leaders at the fort in Kumasi.

In a speech recorded in British colonial dispatches, Hodgson declared that Nana Prempeh would not return and demanded that the Asante hand over the Golden Stool so that he, the Governor, could sit upon it!’
pages.alt: A historical illustration shows the tense meeting outside the Kumasi fort on 28 March 1900 as Asante chiefs listen in stunned silence.

pages.text: Abena gasped. ‘He wanted to sit on the sacred symbol of the nation’s soul?’ ‘Yes,’ said Curator Agyeman. ‘To the Asante, that demand was not just an insult; it was an attempt to destroy the sovereignty and unity of the nation. That evening, the remaining chiefs and Nana Yaa Asantewaa gathered in council to decide how to respond. At first, several chiefs hesitated, fearing the power of British cannons and Maxim guns.’

That evening, the remaining chiefs and Nana Yaa Asantewaa gathered in council to decide how to respond.
At first, several chiefs hesitated, fearing the power of British cannons and Maxim guns.’
pages.alt: In a lamplit council courtyard, Nana Yaa Asantewaa stands upright among hesitating chiefs to speak with courage.

pages.text: ‘What did Nana Yaa Asantewaa say to them?’ asked Kwaku eagerly. ‘No tape recorder existed in nineteen hundred,’ Curator Agyeman explained carefully, ‘so historians do not claim a word-for-word transcript. However, eyewitness oral traditions and early twentieth-century historians record the clear message of her speech: she challenged the chiefs’ hesitation and declared that if the men of Asante would not go forward to defend the Golden Stool, she and the women would stand up to protect it!’

However, eyewitness oral traditions and early twentieth-century historians record the clear message of her speech: she challenged the chiefs’ hesitation and declared that if the men of Asante would not go forward to defend the Golden Stool, she and the women would stand up to protect it!’
pages.alt: Curator Agyeman points to a plaque explaining how oral traditions preserved the meaning of Yaa Asantewaa’s call to courage.

pages.text: ‘Her courage united the council,’ said Curator Agyeman. ‘The chiefs swore an oath to defend the Golden Stool and chose Nana Yaa Asantewaa, then around sixty years old, as Sahene, commander-in-chief of the resistance! For months during the War of the Golden Stool in nineteen hundred, Asante forces built timber stockades, planned strategy, and besieged the British fort in Kumasi.’

For months during the War of the Golden Stool in nineteen hundred, Asante forces built timber stockades, planned strategy, and besieged the British fort in Kumasi.’
pages.alt: A museum diorama shows Nana Yaa Asantewaa in a traditional batakari smock directing strategy with Asante commanders.

pages.text: ‘What happened at the end of the war?’ asked Abena. ‘The British brought thousands of reinforcements and heavy artillery from across West Africa and overseas,’ said Curator Agyeman. ‘Eventually, Nana Yaa Asantewaa and fifteen other leaders were captured and exiled to the Seychelles to join Nana Prempeh the First. She lived there with dignity until she passed away in October nineteen twenty-one.’

She lived there with dignity until she passed away in October nineteen twenty-one.’
pages.alt: An archival sepia portrait in the museum shows Nana Yaa Asantewaa and fellow Asante leaders during their exile in the Seychelles.

pages.text: ‘Did the British ever capture the Golden Stool?’ asked Kwaku. Curator Agyeman smiled. ‘Never! Because of the unity and sacrifice of Nana Yaa Asantewaa and the people, the Golden Stool was kept hidden and safe. Years later, in nineteen twenty-four, Nana Prempeh the First returned home from exile, and today the Golden Stool remains at the heart of Asante heritage and modern Ghana.’

Years later, in nineteen twenty-four, Nana Prempeh the First returned home from exile, and today the Golden Stool remains at the heart of Asante heritage and modern Ghana.’
pages.alt: Curator Agyeman smiles warmly as Kwaku and Abena write notes beside the exhibit of Asante royal heritage.

pages.text: Stepping back into the Kumasi sunshine, Abena looked at her brother. ‘Nana Yaa Asantewaa showed that true leadership is not about seeking comfort,’ she said. ‘It is about standing up for unity, dignity and what matters most when others are afraid.’ Kwaku nodded, closing his notebook carefully. ‘And preserving honest historical evidence ensures her courage will guide Ghana forever.’ The end.

activities.question: How do historians study events from 1900 honestly and accurately?
options: They compare archival records, photos, artefacts and oral traditions
They invent new speeches and pretend they were recorded on tape
They only read stories written in comic books
They guess without checking any dates or places
activities.explanation: Historians cross-check written dispatches, photographs, artefacts, and oral traditions, and distinguish verified facts from summaries.

activities.question: What does the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) represent to the Asante people?
options: The sacred soul, unity and living spirit of the Asante nation
An ordinary wooden chair that anyone can sit on at meetings
A box used for storing British coins
A musical instrument played at markets
activities.explanation: The Golden Stool is never sat upon; it embodies the soul, unity, and spirit of the Asante nation.

activities.question: What triggered the 1900 resistance led by Nana Yaa Asantewaa?
options: Governor Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool to sit on after exiling the King
A heavy rainstorm washed away the roads in Ejisu
The British asked to buy cocoa beans at the market
A dispute over a football match in Kumasi
activities.explanation: Following the 1896 exile of Nana Prempeh I, Governor Hodgson’s March 1900 demand to sit on the Golden Stool sparked the resistance.
